source_title: Criminal Trespass, Second Degree — Unmanned Aircraft Provision
effective_date: 1977 (Laws 1977, LB 38, § 120); unmanned-aircraft subsection (2) added 2009 (Laws 2009, LB238, § 2) and renumbered/amended 2022 (Laws 2022, LB922, § 6)
regulated_party: Any person operating an unmanned aircraft ("electronic device, such as an unmanned aircraft")
regulated_activity: Intentionally causing an unmanned aircraft to enter into, upon, or above the property of another (including property owned by the actor but leased/rented to another) with the intent to observe another person without consent in a place of solitude or seclusion
permit_or_approval_required: No (licensed or privileged entry — not a permit or application process — is the qualifying condition)
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes — directly relevant to any commercial UAS operator whose flight path or camera use could be read as intended to observe a person without consent in a place of solitude or seclusion
aec_relevance: Yes — directly relevant to AEC firms conducting low-altitude mapping, inspection, or construction-monitoring flights near or over private property where incidental observation of occupants in private, secluded areas could occur
summary: Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-521 makes second degree criminal trespass a Class III misdemeanor (Class II if the offender defies a personally communicated order to leave). Subsection (2), added in 2009 and amended in 2022, separately criminalizes intentionally causing an "electronic device, such as an unmanned aircraft," to enter into, upon, or above another's property (including property the actor owns but has leased or rented to another) with intent to observe another person without consent in a place of solitude or seclusion. Subsection (3) defines "unmanned aircraft" as an aircraft, including a drone, operated without the possibility of direct human intervention from within or on the aircraft. No Nebraska appellate decision applying subsection (2) to a UAS-specific fact pattern was located.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Use a mission-specific collection plan for Statewide that limits camera angle, dwell time, audio, zoom, thermal capture, and retention to the contracted purpose. Brief the crew on aborting or redirecting collection when people, residences, or unrelated activity enter the sensor footprint.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Treat Criminal Trespass, Second Degree — Unmanned Aircraft Provision as a documented stop-work or redesign trigger because the packet identifies criminal, civil, evidentiary, or damage exposure. The contract and flight record should preserve the site screening, authority or exception relied upon, crew briefing, and incident/escalation path; obtain counsel where the facts sit near an undefined boundary or intent element.
verification_status: Fetched and read in full directly from nebraskalegislature.gov (official Nebraska Revised Statutes), including source-law citations and case annotations.
notes: Distinct from, and narrower than, the voyeurism-specific unmanned-aircraft provision at § 28-311.08 (NE-002), which addresses viewing/recording a person in a state of undress rather than mere unauthorized entry of the aircraft into airspace over property.

source_title: Unlawful Intrusion; Photograph, Film, or Record Image or Video of Intimate Area — Unmanned Aircraft Provision
effective_date: 1996 (Laws 1996, LB 908, § 1); "unmanned aircraft" language added/amended in subsequent revisions through 2019 (Laws 2019, LB630, § 1)
regulated_activity: Knowingly intruding upon another without consent in a place of solitude or seclusion, where "intrude" is expressly defined to include viewing or recording another person in a state of undress "directly or through electronic or other remote means, including, but not limited to, by unmanned aircraft"
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes, though narrow — applies to any person, commercial or not, whose UAS is used to view or record a person in a state of undress in a place of solitude or seclusion without consent
aec_relevance: Limited but material — relevant primarily as a boundary on incidental imagery capture during aerial mapping, inspection, or construction-monitoring flights near residential structures (e.g., windows, private yards, pools) where a person could be in a state of undress
summary: Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-311.08 makes it unlawful to knowingly intrude upon another without consent in a place of solitude or seclusion (Class I misdemeanor, Class IV felony for a second or subsequent violation), and separately criminalizes knowingly and intentionally photographing, filming, or recording the intimate area of another without knowledge/consent (Class IV felony), and distributing or threatening to distribute such images (felony/misdemeanor tiers). Subsection (8)(b) defines "intrude" to expressly include viewing or recording a person in a state of undress "directly or through electronic or other remote means, including, but not limited to, by unmanned aircraft," and subsection (8)(d) defines "unmanned aircraft" as an aircraft, including a drone, operated without the possibility of direct human intervention from within or on the aircraft. The section was most recently amended by 2026 Laws, LB935, § 19, operative July 18, 2026.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Use a mission-specific collection plan for Statewide that limits camera angle, dwell time, audio, zoom, thermal capture, and retention to the contracted purpose. Brief the crew on aborting or redirecting collection when people, residences, or unrelated activity enter the sensor footprint.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Treat Unlawful Intrusion; Photograph, Film, or Record Image or Video of Intimate Area — Unmanned Aircraft Provision as a documented stop-work or redesign trigger because the packet identifies criminal, civil, evidentiary, or damage exposure. The contract and flight record should preserve the site screening, authority or exception relied upon, crew briefing, and incident/escalation path; obtain counsel where the facts sit near an undefined boundary or intent element.
verification_status: Fetched and read in full directly from nebraskalegislature.gov (official Nebraska Revised Statutes), including the full source-law history and the current July 18, 2026 operative-date notation.
notes: CITATION-DISCREPANCY FLAG: at least one secondary drone-law aggregator cites "Nebraska Revised Statute 28-3115" as the source of this UAS privacy/harassment prohibition. No such statute exists in the current Nebraska Revised Statutes (Chapter 28 does not extend to section 3115; Chapter 28 sections are numbered in the 28-1 to 28-14 range). The correct, verified citation for the UAS-specific voyeurism/intrusion prohibition is § 28-311.08. Do not rely on the "28-3115" citation.

geographic_scope: Statewide (state agencies; political subdivisions "to the extent practicable")
issuing_authority: Nebraska Legislature; administered by NDOT Division of Aeronautics
effective_date: Enacted 2025 (Laws 2025, LB660, §§ 20-24); List of Secure Drones required by 2026-01-01 (§ 73-1005(1)); state-agency purchase restriction and state-funds restriction effective 2027-01-01 (§ 73-1004(1),(3))
binding_level: Binding (statute); state-agency and (to the extent practicable) political-subdivision procurement restriction
regulated_party: State agencies (mandatory); political subdivisions ("to the extent practicable"); NDOT Division of Aeronautics (administers the List); vendors seeking list inclusion
regulated_activity: Purchasing or acquiring a drone/unmanned aerial system; effective January 1, 2027, state agencies may acquire only drones cleared by the Division under the List of Secure Drones Authorized for Purchase, and no state funds may be used to acquire a non-cleared drone
permit_or_approval_required: Not a permit — a List-based purchasing restriction administered by NDOT's Division of Aeronautics; vendors may seek list inclusion by contacting the Division
public_agency_only: Yes — mandatory for state agencies; political subdivisions (counties, cities) must comply "to the extent practicable"; expressly does not regulate private recreational drone use, FAA flight authorization, or non-government purchases per NDOT's own guidance
commercial_operator_relevance: Indirect — does not regulate a private operator's own equipment purchases, but directly affects AEC firms selling UAS equipment/services to, or operating fleets on behalf of, Nebraska state agencies and political subdivisions
aec_relevance: Yes — directly relevant to AEC firms bidding on Nebraska public-agency UAS-inclusive contracts (photogrammetry, inspection, mapping, construction documentation) where agency-furnished or agency-specified equipment must be List-compliant
summary: The Secure Drone Purchasing Act (2025, LB660) directs NDOT's Division of Aeronautics, in consultation with the Department of Administrative Services, the Committee on Pacific Conflict, the Nebraska State Patrol, and the Law Enforcement Drone Association or a comparable organization, to create and maintain a List of Secure Drones Authorized for Purchase by January 1, 2026 (§ 73-1005). Listed drones must be cleared under the U.S. DoD Blue UAS Program, determined NDAA FY2024-compliant, independently determined incapable under normal conditions of transmitting data to unauthorized persons, or otherwise found to present no security threat under detailed cybersecurity/data-protection criteria in § 73-1005(2) (U.S.-based data storage, AES-256 end-to-end encryption, segmented/MFA-controlled networks, tamper-proof hardware, real-time intrusion monitoring, and annual third-party security audits/certifications). Effective January 1, 2027, no state agency may purchase or acquire a drone other than a List-cleared one, and no state funds may be used to acquire a non-cleared drone; a violating contract is void and unenforceable (§ 73-1004). Political subdivisions must comply "to the extent practicable." Electric suppliers in compliance with NERC critical-infrastructure-protection requirements are exempt (§ 73-1004(5)).
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: For public-owner work, confirm before bidding whether the contract extends the List-cleared aircraft and cybersecurity requirements to consultant-furnished systems, and recheck the live list before assigning an aircraft. The statute does not directly regulate an ordinary privately controlled AEC flight merely because the deliverable will be used by a public client.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: NDOT Aeronautics and its statutory partners should keep the authorized-drone list current and preserve the basis for each listing. Agency purchasing staff should retain the list version and security evidence used on the acquisition date and document any political-subdivision practicability determination or statutory exemption.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: Make list eligibility a dated gate at solicitation, award, purchase, and fleet assignment for covered public work beginning January 1, 2027. Retain manufacturer, model, component, data-hosting, encryption, audit, firmware, and funding-source evidence, plus a replacement path if a system is removed from the live list.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: A covered state-agency contract for a non-cleared drone can be void and unenforceable, so identify the purchaser, funding source, acquisition date, and incorporated specification before award. State expressly whether the requirement flows down to a consultant-owned aircraft rather than assuming that a restriction on the public purchaser automatically governs a privately controlled flight.
verification_status: All five sections (§§ 73-1001 to 73-1005) fetched and read in full directly from nebraskalegislature.gov (official Nebraska Revised Statutes); cross-checked against NDOT's own current Aeronautics Division drone-guidance webpage, which links the live List of Secure Drones Authorized for Purchase.
notes: NDOT's guidance page confirms the current List is published at dot.nebraska.gov/aeronautics/drones and is required to be updated at least every six months (§ 73-1005(4)); AEC firms and public-agency clients should recheck the current List before a purchase or specification decision rather than rely on a captured snapshot.

source_title: Foreign Adversary Contracting Prohibition Act — Unmanned Aerial System Definitional Carve-Out
citation: Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 73-901 to 73-908 (2025), as amended by Laws 2025, LB644, §§ 27-30
effective_date: Act originally enacted 2024 (Laws 2024, LB1300); amended by 2025 LB644 (approved by the Governor June 4, 2025), operative 2025-10-01
regulated_party: Public entities (the state, its departments/agencies/political subdivisions, publicly funded higher-education institutions, and persons/entities acting on their behalf) and "scrutinized companies"
regulated_activity: General technology-related contracting: a scrutinized (foreign-adversary-organized, -based, or -controlled) company may not bid on, propose, or contract with a public entity for a "technology-related product or service" (information systems, surveillance, LiDAR, or communications); § 73-903(6), as amended, expressly states this category "does not include unmanned aerial systems"
requirement_type: Contracting prohibition (general) with an express UAS carve-out from that prohibition's scope
commercial_operator_relevance: Indirect — governs public-entity contracting generally, not private operator equipment ownership; AEC firms contracting with Nebraska public entities for non-UAS technology (e.g., LiDAR data services, information systems) should track scrutinized-company certification requirements, but the Act's core restriction does not itself reach UAS procurement
aec_relevance: Yes — AEC firms should understand that Nebraska's general foreign-adversary technology-contracting ban expressly excludes UAS from its "technology-related product or service" definition; Nebraska's UAS-specific procurement security requirements are instead governed by the separate Secure Drone Purchasing Act (NE-003), enacted the same 2025 session
summary: The Foreign Adversary Contracting Prohibition Act (§§ 73-901 to 73-908) bars a "scrutinized company" (one organized in, based in, or controlled by a foreign adversary, or selling a foreign-adversary-originated technology product without incorporating it into another product) from contracting with a Nebraska public entity for a "technology-related product or service," defined as a product/service used for information systems, surveillance, LiDAR, or communications (§ 73-904, § 73-906). As amended by 2025 LB644 (operative October 1, 2025), § 73-903(6)-(7) retains a definition of "unmanned aerial system" but expressly states that the "technology-related product or service" category triggering this Act's contracting ban "does not include unmanned aerial systems." Violating contracts are void; scrutinized companies face civil penalties (the greater of $250,000, twice the contract value, or the public entity's losses) and a five-year contracting ban, enforced by the Attorney General, with a 30% whistleblower reward (§ 73-907). Section 73-908 allows a narrow exception to the general (non-UAS) ban where no reasonable procurement alternative exists and DAS preapproves.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not treat this Act as a Nebraska ban on using a foreign-manufactured UAS: the enacted definition expressly excludes unmanned aerial systems from this Act's restricted technology category. On public work, separately check the Secure Drone Purchasing Act and analyze bundled LiDAR, communications, software, or services that may fall outside the UAS carve-out.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Classify the proposed contract components before applying the scrutinized-company review, separating the UAS itself from independently procured LiDAR, communications, information-system, or surveillance products and services. Preserve the classification and any Department of Administrative Services preapproval used for the Act's no-reasonable-alternative exception.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: Do not use this Act's scrutinized-company restriction as the aircraft eligibility test because UAS are expressly carved out; use the Secure Drone Purchasing Act's live list for covered drone acquisitions. Review separately priced payloads, communications, software, hosting, and other technology services on their own facts rather than assuming the aircraft carve-out covers the entire solution.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Quote and retain the enacted UAS carve-out when correcting specifications or secondary guidance that describes this Act as a drone ban. For bundled procurements, allocate each product and service to the statutory definitions and document any exception before concluding that the entire contract is excluded.
verification_status: Sections 73-901, 73-903 through 73-908 fetched and read in full directly from nebraskalegislature.gov; the enacted LB644 slip-law PDF (approved by the Governor June 4, 2025, operative October 1, 2025) was separately fetched and searched in full for "unmanned," "drone," and specific transition dates.
notes: MAJOR CITATION/SUBSTANCE DISCREPANCY FLAG: multiple secondary/AI-generated summaries (and a brief mention on NDOT's own drone-guidance page) describe LB644 as extending this Act's contracting ban to UAS procurement, asserting that public entities may contract only for UAS procured before July 1, 2026, and may not use UAS procured on or after July 1, 2028. The enacted LB644 text was fetched and searched in full; it contains no reference to "July 1, 2026" or "July 1, 2028" and no UAS-specific contracting ban. Its only UAS-related change is the § 73-903(6)-(7) definitional carve-out EXCLUDING unmanned aerial systems from the Act's core "technology-related product or service" restriction. Treat the July 2026/2028 dates as unverified/likely fabricated by secondary synthesis; do not rely on them. AEC firms and public-entity clients should rely on the Secure Drone Purchasing Act (NE-003) for Nebraska's actual UAS-specific procurement-security regime.

issuing_authority: Nebraska Legislature; enforced by Nebraska Game and Parks Commission
regulated_party: Any person operating an aircraft in connection with hunting or wildlife activity
regulated_activity: Shooting or attempting to shoot at a bird, fish, or other animal while airborne in an aircraft; using an aircraft to harass a bird, fish, or other animal; knowingly participating in such use without a valid § 37-458 permit; shooting/attempting to shoot a coyote from an aircraft under a § 37-458 permit without landowner/tenant permission
requirement_type: Prohibition with a narrow permit exception (§ 37-458, aerial coyote/predator control)
permit_or_approval_required: Yes, for the narrow aerial-predator-control exception (a § 37-458 permit); otherwise no
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes — the Nebraska Game and Parks Commission's own current public guidance (press release most recently republished December 16, 2024, and NDOT's drone-guidance page) states that this statute's "aircraft" prohibition on harassing wildlife is understood by the Commission to include drones/recreational UAS
aec_relevance: Limited but material — relevant to environmental-monitoring, wildlife-survey, or land-management UAS missions in areas where wildlife harassment could be implicated; not applicable to typical mapping/construction/infrastructure-inspection missions absent a wildlife-harassment nexus
summary: Neb. Rev. Stat. § 37-509 makes it a Class II misdemeanor to (a) shoot or attempt to shoot at a bird, fish, or other animal while airborne in any aircraft, (b) use an aircraft to harass any bird, fish, or other animal, (c) knowingly participate in such use without a currently valid § 37-458 permit, or (d) shoot/attempt to shoot a coyote from an aircraft under a § 37-458 permit without first obtaining landowner/tenant permission. The statutory text itself does not define "aircraft" to expressly include unmanned aircraft (unlike some other states' hunting statutes). Nebraska Game and Parks Commission's own public guidance (a press release most recently republished December 16, 2024, and NDOT's Aeronautics drone-guidance webpage) states that state law prohibiting aircraft-based wildlife harassment applies to drones, and separately cautions against drone use near sandhill/whooping cranes, geese, eagles, and state/federally listed species.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Screen the mission for active hunting and wildlife sensitivity within Statewide (wherever wildlife is present/hunted); plan altitude, stand-off distance, route, observers, and abort criteria to avoid pursuit, harassment, surveillance of participants, or assistance to a taking. Document the project's environmental or infrastructure purpose and pause if animals materially react or the flight would disrupt lawful hunting or fishing.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: The ordinary wildlife-harassment prohibition has no application process; the narrow aerial predator-control exception requires a current permit issued under § 37-458, administered by the Nebraska Game and Parks Commission. Confirm the permit, landowner or tenant permission, species, location, dates, participants, and operating conditions before relying on that exception.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 37-509 (2025); a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.
verification_status: Statute fetched and read in full directly from nebraskalegislature.gov; the statute's application to UAS rests on the Game and Parks Commission's own current public guidance rather than an express statutory "aircraft includes unmanned aircraft" definition, so confidence is Moderate rather than High for the UAS-specific application (the underlying statutory prohibition itself is High confidence).
notes: CORRECTED DISCREPANCY: at least one AI-generated secondary summary asserted that Neb. Rev. Stat. § 37-564 (interference with a person hunting, trapping, or fishing) contains a clause reaching "a series of two or more acts using an unmanned aircraft." Section 37-564 was fetched and read in full directly from nebraskalegislature.gov; its current codified text (last amended 1998) contains no reference whatsoever to unmanned aircraft, drones, or UAS. This appears to be a fabricated/hallucinated addition and § 37-564 is not included as a source-register record because it fails the UAS-specific scope gate; do not rely on the secondary claim.

state: Nebraska State Parks, State Historical Parks, State Recreation Areas, and Wildlife Management Areas (NGPC-administered)
jurisdiction_name: Nebraska Game and Parks Commission-administered lands statewide
source_title: Drone Use on Game and Parks Commission Property — Special Occasion Permit Requirement
citation: NGPC public guidance (press release and Special Occasion Permits webpage); cf. Neb. Admin. Code tit. 163, ch. 5, § 001.02 ("Aircraft and Powerless Flight") and tit. 163, ch. 4, § 018 (general Wildlife Management Area property-use rules)
effective_date: Long-standing Commission practice; publicly restated in a press release most recently dated December 16, 2024 (earlier version circulated around 2018); Special Occasion Permits webpage last modified per site metadata 2023-06-29
revision_date: Restated December 16, 2024 (press release); webpage current as of access date
binding_level: Official agency policy / permit condition (not itself a UAS-specific codified administrative rule)
regulated_party: Any person operating a drone on Commission-administered property
regulated_activity: Flying a drone in a state park, state historical park, state recreation area, or wildlife management area
requirement_type: Prohibition subject to a Special Occasion Permit
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — a Special Occasion Permit, applied for at least 30 days before the planned activity, through the nearest Commission district office (commercial photography/videography additionally requires a Special Occasion Production Amendment)
aec_relevance: Yes — directly relevant to any AEC firm planning UAS mapping, inspection, or documentation work on Commission-administered park, historical park, recreation-area, or WMA land
summary: Nebraska Game and Parks Commission's current public guidance states that the Commission does not permit drones to be flown in state parks, state historical parks, state recreation areas, or wildlife management areas unless a Special Occasion Permit has been approved (application submitted at least 30 days before the event, through the nearest Commission district office); commercial photography/videography additionally requires a Special Occasion Production Amendment. The codified Nebraska Administrative Code provisions governing these properties — Title 163, Chapter 5, § 001.02 ("Aircraft and Powerless Flight," prohibiting aircraft operation/landing outside designated areas and air-delivery of persons/objects without prior written Commission permission) and Title 163, Chapter 4, § 018 (general Wildlife Management Area property-use rules) — were reviewed in full and contain no reference to "drone," "unmanned," or "UAS" by name; their general "aircraft" language predates UAS-specific terminology.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat property authorization for Statewide (NGPC-administered park and WMA lands) as a pre-mobilization gate and obtain conditions that cover launch, landing, route, dates, aircraft, crew, and sensor purpose. Confirm whether the approval is site-wide or location-specific and carry the written authorization and field contact with the crew.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Direct the applicant to the nearest Nebraska Game and Parks Commission district office for the Special Occasion Permit at least 30 days before the operation, and require the production amendment for commercial photography or videography when applicable. The written approval should identify the property, operating area, dates, aircraft, purpose, conditions, and field contact.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under NGPC public guidance (press release and Special Occasion Permits webpage); cf. Neb. Admin. Code tit. 163, ch. 5, § 001.02 ("Aircraft and Powerless Flight") and tit. 163, ch. 4, § 018 (general Wildlife Management Area property-use rules); a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.
verification_status: The Commission's press release and Special Occasion Permits webpage were fetched and read in full directly from outdoornebraska.gov (official Commission site); the codified Title 163 rules were separately fetched and reviewed in full via Justia's official Administrative Code mirror and confirmed to contain no UAS-specific text. Confidence is Moderate because current agency practice (permit requirement) is verified directly, but it is not itself expressed in the named codified rule text, creating a gap between the agency's stated practice and the administrative rule's plain wording.
notes: Reverse of the discrepancy pattern flagged in other states in this program (e.g., Montana's repealed park drone rule): here the current codified administrative rule was never UAS-specific, but the agency's own current, repeatedly restated public guidance imposes a clear drone permit requirement in practice. AEC firms should confirm requirements directly with the relevant Commission district office before flying, since the binding legal basis for the permit requirement (as opposed to the agency's stated practice) was not independently pinned down to a specific UAS-named rule provision in this pass.

source_title: Drones in Nebraska: Rules, Safety, and Secure Purchasing (NDOT Aeronautics)
citation: dot.nebraska.gov/aeronautics/drones (official NDOT webpage); administering agency for the Secure Drone Purchasing Act (NE-003)
revision_date: Continuously updated; reviewed as of access date
binding_level: Advisory guidance (for private/commercial operators); official agency administration (for the List of Secure Drones under NE-003)
uas_topic: State aviation office UAS guidance; procurement-list administration; agency drone-use description
regulated_party: General public and commercial UAS operators (guidance); state agencies and vendors (List of Secure Drones administration)
regulated_activity: Provides FAA-compliance signposting (Part 107, registration, Remote ID, LAANC, TFRs); publishes and administers the List of Secure Drones Authorized for Purchase under the Secure Drone Purchasing Act; describes NDOT's own UAS uses (bridge/culvert inspection, project documentation and mapping, emergency response, environmental and right-of-way monitoring)
permit_or_approval_required: No formal permit for private operators; vendors seeking List of Secure Drones inclusion may contact the Aeronautics Division directly (402-471-2371)
public_agency_only: No (guidance is public-facing); Yes (as to the binding force of the List of Secure Drones itself, per NE-003)

aec_relevance: Yes — illustrates the kind of public-agency AEC-adjacent UAS work occurring in Nebraska and is the authoritative current source for the Secure Drone Purchasing Act's evolving List of Secure Drones
summary: NDOT's Aeronautics Division maintains a public webpage consolidating Nebraska UAS rules: it summarizes the Secure Drone Purchasing Act and links the current List of Secure Drones Authorized for Purchase (updated at least every six months per statute); summarizes the Foreign Adversary Contracting Prohibition Act's application to government drone procurement with public funds; references the criminal trespass statute (§ 28-521) and Game and Parks Commission park/WMA drone restrictions; and reiterates FAA baseline requirements (Part 107 or TRUST certification, registration, Remote ID, LAANC/DroneZone authorization). practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Use the NDOT page as a current navigation aid for Nebraska-specific preflight screening, then verify each applicable restriction or permission against the linked statute, live secure-drone list, or Game and Parks process. For an NDOT assignment, reconcile aircraft eligibility, data handling, inspection or mapping deliverables, and emergency deconfliction requirements with the executed scope before mobilization.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: NDOT Aeronautics should keep the consolidated guidance and authorized-drone list synchronized with statutory changes and clearly distinguish federal reminders, binding Nebraska rules, and agency practice. Project staff should direct contractors to the controlling specification or approval rather than treating the overview page itself as a project authorization.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: Use the live NDOT authorized-drone list—not a saved vendor claim—as the starting eligibility check for a covered public acquisition, then verify the specific model, components, data path, encryption, audit evidence, firmware, and mission software. Record the list date and acceptance-test configuration so later list or software changes can trigger reassessment.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Treat the NDOT webpage as consolidated guidance rather than an independent source of new prohibitions, and cite the underlying statute, list, permit, or contract term for each mandatory condition. Resolve the page's imprecise description of the Foreign Adversary Contracting Prohibition Act by relying on the enacted UAS carve-out and the separate Secure Drone Purchasing Act.
